item.title: Needs work to satisfy my anal retentive-ness
item.content:encoded:
I think it should go back much further, like to the Ming or Tang dynasties, back when China was something other than a prize to be divvied up by foreign powers. In that same vein, I would be interested to see him attempt to link some of the traits to Chinese natural philosophy of the day, rather than what appears to be essentially western science1.

I did like the bit about the huts now being property of the Emperor, although it muddied up the role of Mr. Weilun. The article initially made it seem as though he was a largely single explorer doing his thing and sending stuff back to the Emprah, but the thing with the huts made it seem as though he was acting in some official capacity. If he was, it would make more sense for him to have a large and glorious retinue to show the awesome might of the Emperor of the Middle Kingdom, just as Zhang He did. As it is, he seems to be essentially a reskinned version of Wordsworth/Blackwood/every other 19th century "gentleman explorer" real or otherwise.

Now for random, unorganized thoughts

  • the loldenda at the very end is unnecessary
  • "Dr. ███████ suspects an E-class reality incursion."

Don't care. Speculation of this nature seems kind of pointless.

  • I don't much care for the zoo being open to the public, as part of my problem with this being a version of Victorian adventurers, but with Chinese names.
  • If you wanted to Zheng He him to the max, you could also have him send back religious artifacts, new spices/cultivars unrelated to any found on Earth, etc.
  • A thought occurs, but it's not super hashed out, so make of it what you wish: What if this guy was one of several vying for the favor of the Emperor? Like, a faction of, say Supreme Clarity Daoists or Pure Land Buddhists or whatever decided to catch the ear of the Emperor by sending him the most fanciful gifts and creatures imaginable and claim the lands of foreign barbarians in his name? They send out their best and brightest to do it. But the Emperor dies and the faction is eventually forgotten. But this fellow and his men are still out there in the cosmos, sending gifts which they feel might be pleasing to His Highness. Hell, for all we know, there could be even more of these things just waiting to be discovered, all filled with creatures from [DATA EXPUNGED] and with helpful little descriptions interspersed with suggestions and supplications to the Emperor to keep the Buddha/Lao-Tzu/Jesus in his heart.
  • Also, if this is for TEH EMPRAH, he would probably send back only beautiful or pleasing species, not necessarily the beetle that shoots flesh-dissolving acid when looked at, even if it is a vital part of the ecosystem.

It could be a colossal pain in the ass to work out, but it's a thought.

At any rate, as you have it written now, it's not significantly different enough from the original to have me change my not-vote.

Footnotes
1. It might also be worthwhile to look into early Chinese Buddhist travelers such as Faxien and Xuanzang, as well as Ibn Battuta and Sir John Mandeville

item.content:encoded:
Before this gets taken down for re-work, he's some suggestions:

"Genetic link ascertains a relation"

Very awkward phrasing here. I can help you with rewording, if you like, but here's an attempt: "Genetic sequencing reveals closest living relative to be Elephas maximus, the Asian elephant, with a divergence time between 1 million and 700,000 years ago."

"…very large decapodal invertebrate"

Are we talking house-sized or car-sized or 4-year-old-sized?

"Para-Amazon"

Love that.

"…remains stored in formaldehyde"

Biological specimens are stored in ~90% ethanol, not formaldehyde. The formaldehyde/formalin is a fixing agent applied briefly (on the order of a few hours to a few days, depending) before putting the specimen in alcohol. I recommend changing wording to "remains fixed in formalin and stored in 90% ethanol."

item.title: A thing I wrote this evening
item.content:encoded:
Thought about some of the criticism I recieved when writing this article, and I tried to expand the subject logs because some people wanted to see more information there. At present, Woodsworth is still Wordsworth, although his name might change to Philippe Dupont depending.

As you can tell, Woodsworth is less of a big game hunter and more of a thoughtful naturalist, akin to Huxley or Charles Darwin, who is developing a theory based on all the various animals he has viewed across space and time and sent back to captivity.

 Extended Acquisitions log as of █/██/█████  
Close

Date Acquired: 09/15/20██
Species: unknown, described as “lesser bugbladder”.
Description: Three large (approx.15 ft long) ground-dwelling invertebrates protected by chitinous armour. No eyes present, but several highly developed antennae and vibrissae indicate highly developed senses of smell and touch. When threatened, it releases a noxious gas composed of eight volatile components, creating a foul smell.
Current Status: Stored at Bio-Site 29.
Exerpt from Manual 091520██:

“This odiferous creature is a fascinating example of predator/prey relations. Deprived of eyes, this organism insead reacts to threatening stimuli with a unique chemical defense like that of Earth skunks. If any individual were born without such a defense, they would be swiftly quashed by the bugbladder's natural predators. […] Store in large,dark habitat mimicking a limestone cave, if possible. They enjoy eating loose topsoil lined with potassium- I believe that they consume small organisms and fungi as they churn the soil.”

Date Acquired: 09/21/20██
Species: unknown, described as “dimpled tunnelworm”
Description: Large (approx. 20 ft long) soft-bodied invertebrate similar to an earthworm. Though it possesses no eyes, the creature is extremely sensitive to vibrations. It is believed to hunt by tracking vibrations and smelling prey with the eight large spiracles that surround its mouth.
Current status: Stored at Bio-Site 29. Possible relocation to Site ██ pending as growth rates increase.
Excerpt from Manual 092120██:

“Though it rarely surfaces, an adult tunnelworm breaching the topsoil is an awe-inspiring sight, far more than a lowly earthworm which it resembles. During my stay on [REDACTED], I witnessed several tunnelworms surface and deposit eggs to be fertilized in typical invertebrate fashion. I believe that this courtship behaviour has something to do with the solar eclipse that occurred that day, as very few animals on this world ever leave the large caverns in which they make their homes. It is possible that baby tunnelworms spend their lives in the uppermost layers of soil, with few predators to menace them […] Capturing this beast proved to be a chore. We eventually lured an infant specimen out into a cavern by dragging a dead bugbladder through a tunnel, while simultaneously pounding on the cavern wall with a large sledgehammer! Restraining the beast should be easy enough provided that it is given ample food and soil- I suspect that slaughterhouse offal can provide a temporary substitute for wild bugbladders. The three bugbladders that I have already sent to you should be kept well away from this one, as you should no doubt realize.”

Date Acquired: 09/27/20██
Species: unknown, described as “Barnabus’s cave crab”
Description: Two large invertebrates (approx. 2 feet in diameter), superficially resembling a brachyurid crustacean. Possesses ten limbs, with four (4) of these limbs adapted into grasping appendages with a rudimentary “thumb” and two “fingers”. Primarily aquatic. Specimen spends long periods of time in a sedentary state at the bottom of its containment tank without need of food.
Current status: Stored at Bio-site 29. 11/11/20██, the two organisms reproduced via external fertilization. Several days later, one subject (believed to be female) killed and ate her mate. Specimen was relocated to a larger tank. Eggs remain under study.
Excerpt from Manual 092720██:

“Cave crabs seem to live largely sedentary lives, spending most of their time lying motionless on the shores of the underground lakes waiting for prey, which is then dissected, almost clinically, by their four claws. There appears to be no upward growth to their limit; the largest cave crab we encountered measured almost fourteen meters across and had become covered with bioluminescent fungi. Cave crabs prey primarily on aquatic invertebrates and I suspect that a suitable alternative in captivity would include crayfish or krill. Despite living on another world, Barnabus’s cave crab (so named after my dear departed colleague Dr. Barnabus Jorgenson) seems to have taken the same shape as many of our terrestrial crabs. Is this the process of a greater Designer, who has populated space and time with only the most efficient and well-designed creatures, or have natural pressures moulded two unrelated organisms into shapes that fit a similar niche? Many clergymen and bishops believe the former, but as I continue my expeditions I have begun to suspect the latter.”

  • "fifty (50)" - ditch the parenthetical; the number you're speaking of is approximate anyway.
  • "At irregular intervals, animals will appear… These animals appear <snip> at random intervals." — Two sentences in a row saying the same thing.

I had a headache with pictures that unfortunately would only work with Blackwood II: Electric Boogaloo. Namely, an obviously sentient species that has been imprisoned as well. Think Victorian-era exhibitions of pygmies (or hell, the Wild West Show, for that matter). Un/fortunately, Jacques Cousteau (or his otherworldly equivalent) seems too humane to do something so obviously awful.

Also, going a bit off of what wishun said, it should be noted somewhere that while the intervals between new arrivals are generally random, they do attend to arrive in "batches." If you're on the savannah of a planet with an ammonium atmosphere, you're going to try to retrieve as many specimens of the various fauna as possible before heading off to sub-arctic climes of the planet with 1% of Earth's gravity.

Also also, perhaps attempts are made by the "zookeeper" to recreate the environment of the species by shipping them back with indigenous flora as well as the instructions about feeding, atmosphere, etc.? As with all things in life, my guide for this is Jacques Cousteau, and that seems like something he would do, at least moreso than sticking the majestic fifty-horned gazelle in a barren cage.

  • Extend care and feeding guides for the various animals.

Any other suggestions?

The zoo itself, described as a "Collection of Curiosities" is named for a “William Woodsworth”, billed as “the greatest explorer and naturalist this side of Reality 12/3.14.” According to promotional materials found within SCP-257, the zoo was founded in 1899 to “educate the gentlemen and ladies of England about Nature, and the many strange Beasts encountered by Explorers on their Travels.” No permits, building licences, or planning permissions have been found that correspond to the location or appearance of SCP-257.

Holy quotations man. I don't even know why there needs to be here. Especially on last quote here, it just doesn't seem necessary to the article in any way.

Several signs and notices indicate that the zoo has been “temporarily closed for maintenance”, but the dilapidated appearance of the park and outdated equipment suggests that the park has been abandoned for at least fifty (50) years.

Dude you don't even need the quoting over here; it's perfectly fine without it and actually reads smoother without it.

At irregular intervals, animals will appear within the zoo’s confines through an unknown manner.

The fact that what it does appears 3rd paragraph in the description annoys me to no end.

This just doesn't do it for me. Downboat.

item.content:encoded:
Sorry. You don't own "old timey Englishman explorer has fantastical adventures." And I'll be honest, that wasn't an original idea on the part of Lord Blackwood, either. What made Lord Blackwood stand out was the fact that he's a sea slug that's also an old timey Englishman explorer. You added a twist to a trope that was established back in the 19th century. You didn't invent it. As such, your assertion that this article is, not just is like Lord Blackwood is pretty baseless.

I'll go further and say that it's unfair to the author that you're coming into the discussion thread and accusing him of ripping you off (and adding in the same characterization of SCP-1958 for good measure), when there is no evidence of that being true at all. Plagiarism, whether literal or conceptual, is a pretty serious charge to throw around, and if you're going to accuse someone of it, I think it requires a higher standard of evidence than what you're offering.
